import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Lychrel numbers in base 10

A (base-10) *Lychrel number* is a positive integer which never becomes a palindrome under the
iteration

$$a_{0} = n, \qquad a_{k+1} = a_k + \operatorname{rev}_{10}(a_k).$$

One commonly stated conjectural direction is that there are no Lychrel numbers in base 10.
The smallest widely studied open case is `196`.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
* [MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
* [OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
* [OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
-/

namespace LychrelNumbers

/-- The base (10) used for digit reversal. -/
abbrev base : ℕ := 10

/--
The digit-reversal map $\operatorname{rev}_{10}(n)$.

Implementation note: `Nat.digits base n` returns the digits of `n` in *little-endian* order.
Reversing this list and interpreting it again as little-endian digits gives the usual digit
reversal.
-/
def rev10 (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.ofDigits base (Nat.digits base n).reverse

/-- A number is a (base-10) palindrome if it equals its digit reversal. -/
def IsPalindrome10 (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  rev10 n = n

/-- One step of the Lychrel iteration: `n ↦ n + rev10 n`. -/
def lychrelStep (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  n + rev10 n

/-- The number $n$ is a (base-10) Lychrel number if no iterate of the Lychrel process is a palindrome. -/
def IsLychrel10 (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ k : ℕ, ¬ IsPalindrome10 (lychrelStep^[k] n)

/--
**Lychrel conjecture (base 10):** conjecturally, there are no Lychrel numbers in base 10.

Equivalently, every positive integer eventually becomes a palindrome under the Lychrel iteration.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem no_lychrel_numbers_base10 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ¬ IsLychrel10 n := by
  sorry

/--
The first widely studied open case: whether `196` is a base-10 Lychrel number.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem isLychrel10_196 : answer(sorry) ↔ IsLychrel10 196 := by
  sorry

/-- An equivalent formulation of `no_lychrel_numbers_base10`. -/
@[category API, AMS 11]
theorem eventually_palindrome_base10 :
    (∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ∃ k : ℕ, IsPalindrome10 (lychrelStep^[k] n)) ↔
      (∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ¬ IsLychrel10 n) := by
  constructor
  · intro h n hn hn_lychrel
    rcases h n hn with ⟨k, hk⟩
    exact hn_lychrel k hk
  · intro h n hn
    by_contra hcontra
    have : IsLychrel10 n := by
      intro k hk
      exact hcontra ⟨k, hk⟩
    exact h n hn this


/-- Sanity check: digit reversal of `120` is `21`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem rev10_120 : rev10 120 = 21 := by
  native_decide

/-- Sanity check: `121` is a base-10 palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem palindrome_121 : IsPalindrome10 121 := by
  dsimp [IsPalindrome10]
  native_decide

/-- Sanity check: `56 → 121` in one Lychrel step. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem lychrelIter_56_one : lychrelStep^[1] 56 = 121 := by
  native_decide

/-- Sanity check: the Lychrel iteration at `56` reaches a palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem eventually_palindrome_56 : ∃ k : ℕ, IsPalindrome10 (lychrelStep^[k] 56) := by
  refine ⟨1, ?_⟩
  dsimp [IsPalindrome10]
  native_decide
end LychrelNumbers

findings.description: The quantifier `∀ k : ℕ` includes k = 0, so this predicate requires the starting number itself to be nonpalindromic. More precisely, it is equivalent to `¬ IsPalindrome10 n ∧ (∀ k, ¬ IsPalindrome10 (lychrelStep^[k + 1] n))`. Consequently, Lean immediately proves `¬ IsLychrel10 4994` and `¬ IsLychrel10 9999`, whereas under the convention allowing palindromic starts these are unresolved candidates, not numbers excluded by definition. This is questionable rather than a definite misformalization because the references explicitly document both conventions. Neither open theorem is affected, as the equivalences recorded below show.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number, section “Threads, seed and kin numbers”: “A seed number may be a palindrome itself.” The primary terminology page https://www.p196.org/html/definitions.html explicitly says “A Lychrel number MAY BE a palindrome itself.” Conversely, OEIS A023108, comment by M. F. Hasler dated April 13, 2019, says it is unclear whether palindromes are excluded and points to the distinct conventions in A088753 and A063048. MathWorld’s linked 196-Algorithm article also counts an initially palindromic number as requiring zero iterations.
findings.suggested_fix: Choose and explicitly document the convention. To match the palindrome-allowing convention, define `IsLychrel10 n := ∀ k : ℕ, ¬ IsPalindrome10 (lychrelStep^[k + 1] n)` and use the corresponding positive iterates in the API equivalence. Alternatively, retain the current predicate but identify it explicitly as the zero-iteration convention and cite the appropriate variant.

reformulations.difference: The right-hand side negates the zero-inclusive Lychrel predicate rather than directly requiring every positive starting value to produce a palindrome after at least one reverse-and-add step.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Write F = lychrelStep and P = IsPalindrome10. Classical quantifier negation gives `(∀ n > 0, ¬ IsLychrel10 n) ↔ (∀ n > 0, ∃ k ≥ 0, P(F^[k] n))`. Since F(n) = n + rev10(n) is positive whenever n is positive, apply the latter universal assertion to F(n). A witness k then gives P(F^[k+1] n), hence a positive-time palindrome. The converse simply allows the same positive-time witness among all natural times. Thus the theorem faithfully asks the universal-palindrome question under either convention. These equivalences were proved in the scratch file without using either admitted research theorem.

reformulations.difference: The predicate tests iteration zero as well as the positive iterations used by the palindrome-allowing convention.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The scratch proof establishes `IsLychrel10 n ↔ ¬ IsPalindrome10 n ∧ (∀ k, ¬ IsPalindrome10 (lychrelStep^[k+1] n))`. For n = 196, the extra conjunct is true because rev10(196) = 691 ≠ 196. Therefore the two formulations of the 196 question are equivalent.

could_not_verify: LychrelNumbers.IsLychrel10: the references do not impose a single convention for palindromic starting values. Pointwise equivalence of the two predicates was not established; this uncertainty is reported as the questionable finding above. The faithfulness of both open theorem statements was verified independently.
review.notes: Checked every declaration, the answer-slot scopes, positivity, and boundary cases. Digit reversal and all four sanity-check statements are correct; numeric palindrome equality was also proved equivalent to palindromicity of the canonical digit list. The API equivalence is correctly proved and does not assume either open theorem. Both research-open tags agree with the sources. MathWorld records the historical universal-palindrome conjecture, so the unanswered no-Lychrel question was not treated as a reversed mathematical answer. OEIS web pages were blocked, but their full entries were obtained from the official OEIS data mirror.
